chunks: Ahmad ibn Idrees and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kufi, from Ibn Faddal, from one of our companions, from Sa'd al-Iskaf, who said:

I came to Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام) seeking permission to enter upon him, and there were camel saddles lined up at the door, and the voices had risen. Then a group came out wearing turbans, resembling the Zutt.

He said: So I entered upon Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام) and said: May I be made your ransom, your permission for me was delayed today, and I saw a people come out before me wearing turbans, and I did not recognize them. He said: Do you know who those are, O Sa'd? He said: I said: No. He said: They are your brothers from the jinn. They come to us and ask us about their halal (permissible) and their haram (forbidden), and the features of their religion.

key_terms.أَبَا جَعْفَرٍ: Imam Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام), the one being visited and consulted
key_terms.الْجِنِّ: the jinn, unseen beings who came seeking religious guidance
key_terms.الْعَمَائِمِ: turbans, describing the appearance of the visiting group
key_terms.حَرَامِهِمْ: their forbidden matters according to religious law
key_terms.حَلَالِهِمْ: their permissible matters according to religious law
key_terms.مَعَالِمِ دِينِهِمْ: the teachings and defining features of their religion

ai.seo_question: Did the jinn come to the Imams (عليهم السلام) to ask about halal and haram?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates that a group who appeared unfamiliar to Sa'd al-Iskaf had just visited Imam Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام). The Imam explained that they were brethren from the jinn who came to ask the Imam about their halal, haram, and the teachings of their religion. The report highlights the religious authority of the Imam and the extension of guidance even to the jinn.
